snapshot.title: UPSC Economy: External Sector & BOP
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC Economy Finale Hook: Current: Goods/Services/Remit. Capital: FDI/FPI/Loans. CAD: India's reality. Hot Money: FPI. Tarapore: Convertibility.

quick_notes.title: Balance of Payments (BOP)
quick_notes.detail: A systematic record of all economic transactions of a country with the rest of the world. Always balances in accounting terms.
quick_notes.explanation: Balance of Payments (BOP) is a complete record of all money and goods that flow between a country and other countries over a specific time period, such as a year. This record includes things like exports and imports of goods and services, money sent home by workers abroad, foreign investments, and loans from other nations. The BOP always balances in accounting terms because every transaction that brings money into the country (a credit) is matched by a transaction that sends money out (a debit), even if the total amounts are not equal in reality. For example, if a country imports more than it exports, the difference is covered by borrowing from other countries or using its foreign currency reserves, so the books still balance.

quick_notes.title: Current Account
quick_notes.detail: Transactions of goods (Trade balance), services (Invisibles), and transfers (Remittances). India usually has a Current Account Deficit (CAD) due to oil/gold imports.
quick_notes.explanation: The current account is a record of a country's transactions with the rest of the world, covering three main parts: trade in goods, which is called the trade balance; trade in services, also known as invisibles; and money transfers, such as remittances sent home by workers abroad. When the value of imports of goods, services, and transfers is greater than exports, the country runs a current account deficit, or CAD. India frequently has a CAD because it spends a lot on importing crude oil and gold.

quick_notes.title: Capital Account
quick_notes.detail: Transactions involving assets and liabilities. Includes FDI, FPI, External Commercial Borrowings (ECB), and NRI deposits.
quick_notes.explanation: The Capital Account is a part of a country's balance of payments, which is a record of all money coming into and going out of the country. It specifically tracks transactions involving assets and liabilities, meaning it records the buying and selling of things that hold value, like shares of a company or real estate. For example, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is when a foreign company builds a factory in India, and Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) is when a foreign investor buys Indian stocks or bonds. It also includes External Commercial Borrowings (ECB), which are loans taken by Indian companies from foreign lenders, and Non-Resident Indian (NRI) deposits, which are money that Indians living abroad put into Indian bank accounts. Unlike the Current Account, which records daily trade in goods and services, the Capital Account shows changes in a country's ownership of long-term financial assets and debts.

quick_notes.title: FDI vs FPI
quick_notes.detail: FDI (Foreign Direct Investment): Stable, long-term, >10% stake, management control. FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investment): Volatile, "Hot Money", <10% stake.
quick_notes.explanation: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is when a foreign investor buys more than 10% of a company's shares, giving them a long-term stake and some control over how the company is managed. This type of investment is considered stable because it usually stays in the country for many years. Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) is when a foreign investor buys less than 10% of a company's shares, often to make quick profits from short-term price changes. Because FPI can be sold and moved out of a country very quickly, it is called "hot money" and is very volatile, meaning it can fluctuate wildly. So the key difference is that FDI is long-term and brings management control, while FPI is short-term and purely for financial gain.

quick_notes.title: Rupee Convertibility
quick_notes.detail: Current Account: Fully convertible. Capital Account : Partially convertible (to prevent sudden flight of capital). Tarapore Committee reports.
quick_notes.explanation: Rupee convertibility means how freely you can exchange Indian rupees for foreign currencies like US dollars. The current account is the part of India's international trade that includes payments for goods, services (like tourism or software), and income transfers (like money sent home by workers); this account is fully convertible, so you can exchange rupees for foreign currency for these purposes without government permission. However, the capital account involves large investments like buying stocks, real estate, or setting up factories in another country; this account is only partially convertible, meaning the government restricts how much money can move in or out to prevent sudden flight of capital—where investors quickly pull their money out of India, causing economic instability. The Tarapore Committee reports, named after chairman S.S. Tarapore, provided recommendations in 1997 and 2006 on how India could safely move toward full capital account convertibility, but full convertibility has not been adopted yet. So, for everyday needs like studying abroad or importing goods, the rupee is freely exchangeable, but for large cross-border investments, approvals or limits still apply.
